"Well, Mr. Fluffykins?! What do you say to this?!"

With a flourish, you tossed a brown envelope onto the table. A few papers slid out, revealing various pictures of cats, each more peculiar than the last. One was a cat sitting at a piano, its paw poised over the keys as if about to play a dramatic solo in a silent film. 

"Conclusive proof," you declared, leaning back in your chair with a mix of relief and astonishment etched on your face. "An alien life form has been using common house cats as hosts to gather information about the human race."

Dr. Amelia Hart, your esteemed colleague, adjusted her glasses, her eyes scanning the documents with meticulous care. "These images... they're astonishing," she murmured, picking up the picture of the feline musician. "But you've managed to document this, haven't you?"

"Indeed," you replied, smiling with a sense of pride. "Years of relentless research have led to this moment. Each image is accompanied by detailed analysis. There are changes in cat behavior—increased vocalization, strange patterns in play, and these... enhancements. They're not just pets anymore."

"I figure you should be twenty-one by now." The words on the page tremble slightly as I try and read. "If not, you should complain to the package service; I paid good money to make sure this got there on time."

I hold the letter close, the handwriting oddly familiar, yet it must belong to someone else. The postmark tells me it's been sitting in my mailbox for days, but I only noticed it today. My heart hammers against my ribcage as I unfold the envelope more carefully, as if my brother might step out from the shadow and laugh at my surprise.

The package inside is modest, a square box wrapped in sturdy brown paper, the twine binding it tight. My fingers fumble as I cut through the string, a piece snapping too quickly and scraping my skin. I ignore the tiny cut, peeling back the paper to reveal a nondescript box with no markings.

The letter continues, a peculiar blend of humor and solemnity:

"Inside, you’ll find something small, perhaps insignificant. But I want you to have it. These things I'm sending may not bring me back, but they might help you understand a little more about who I was and who you're becoming."

I lift the lid, my breath hitching as my fingers graze something soft.

I'm still not certain exactly how it happened, but to be honest, I'm okay with that. All I know is that one minute I was driving home after a long day at work, and the next, I found myself at a quaint, little café I'd never noticed before tucked away at the edge of a bustling street. The name, "The Endless Brew," seemed oddly fitting, given the circumstances. 

I pulled up a stool at the bar, my hands still shaking slightly from stress. The barista, a jovial man with a gentle smile, asked what I wanted. Coffee, black, I said automatically. He nodded and turned to prepare my drink. That's when I noticed the elderly man seated next to me, a regular by the looks of it, sipping away at his coffee. His mug was enormous, steaming, and topped with an excessive amount of creamer. It surprised me how much creamer Death put in his coffee.

Death? I blinked, confused. The man glanced over, his eyes twinkling mischievously beneath his hat. "You'll get used to it," he murmured, a hint of a smile playing on his lips.

Before I could question him, my own coffee arrived, steaming hot and inviting. I took a sip, and just like that, my world seemed to tilt on its axis. The coffee was incredible – rich, smooth, and with a hint of sweetness that wasn't coming from sugar. I looked at the barista, and then back at my cup, puzzled. He simply smiled knowingly.

I turned to the elderly gentleman, curious. "Why...why do you put so much creamer in your coffee?" I asked.

He chuckled, a sound like wind chimes in the breeze.

I remember my first days as a doctor. I wore my stethoscope proudly around my neck, not realizing it advertised how much of a virgin I was in the field of medicine. I'd introduce myself as Dr. Agon and tried to mask my inexperience with determination and a polite smile. The hospital corridors were my labyrinth, every corner held a new challenge to face with a resolve built from endless hours of studying.

But as time passed, the grind of the hospital began to wear on me. The endless demands, the sleepless nights, the ungratefulness of some patients—all the things I'd imagined as noble causes started to feel like a relentless cycle of despair. It was a slow erosion, day by day.

One evening, I was on call in the emergency department when a particularly gruesome car accident came in. A multiple-casualty incident; the kind they drill you for but never quite prepare you for in reality. Amidst the chaos, I managed to save a young girl, her fragile body battered but alive. It was a moment that should have filled me with pride, but instead, I found myself drained, emotionally and physically.

That night, I stood at the hospital's rooftop, gazing at the city lights blinking in the dark, and made a decision. My life as a doctor, I decided, was to be no longer about selfless service, but about power—the power to control life and death. It was a crossroads I never knew I'd reach, and I veered sharply off the path I had sworn to walk.

I started to exploit my position for personal gain.

He heard the shouting before he saw them coming. The din reverberated through the halls of creation, bouncing off the walls of eternity. Annoyed at the disturbance, God took one look out the window and groaned. He reached for his aspirin – it had earned a spot in every room he owned – and plodded downstairs to the foyer.

Out in the colosseum-like arena crafted from the very matter of his will, the sky cracked with crimson and gold as sun and storm mingled to set the stage for the day's gruesome spectacles. Here, he had crafted humanity through the process of natural selection, sculpting a species into the ultimate killing machines. Each creature, designed with predatory instincts sharp as a blade and bodies honed for battle, now clashed in a brutal ballet of survival.

As he watched, bloodlust filled the air, a thick miasma of desire and death. There were the massive brutes, built like ancient war machines, their muscles coiled and ready to strike. There were the swift and cunning, moving like shadows, striking from the unseen. And then there were the bizarre anomalies, creatures of circumstance shaped by quirks of the genetic dice roll, adding an unpredictable edge to the deadly contests.

God shook his head, a mix of pride and trepidation swelling within him. "What have I done?" he murmured. "I created them to entertain... and perhaps to outwit the other gods who took sport in such bloody games."

The tournaments were indeed gladiatoresque in nature, only God's versions were far beyond the mortal realms of Rome's past.

I leaned my rifle against the bed and put my backpack on, and as I was reaching for my rifle again the whole house rocked, and I heard a series of impacts in every direction. More landing pods of course. If the emergency operator had called out any information, it was lost in the chaos of the attack. The intruders were here, and from the sound of the impacts, they were in force.

I grabbed my rifle, checking it was loaded, and slipped on my ballistic vest. Each piece of gear felt like armor against the imminent threat. I hustled through the house, making sure every door was locked, every window boarded or shuttered. The voice on the phone had been curt, no room for hesitation or doubt.

I peered out a crack in the curtains. The streets were a battlefield, littered with debris, and smoke billowed from several points where the enemy's landing pods had touched down. Civilians screamed in the distance, a harrowing soundtrack to the unfolding nightmare.

The voice echoed in my head, "Good luck and God bless." I clung to those words, a lifeline in the storm. I whispered a prayer under my breath and took up a position by the bedroom window, peering through the sights of my rifle. My heart hammered in my chest, but my hands remained steady.

As I waited, every sound was amplified – a car alarm blaring in the distance, a dog barking in fright, the sudden silence which always precedes the next move in a war. Then I saw them – silhouettes against the smoky sky, moving with purpose and menace.

I took a deep breath, focused on my targets. Shooting was not something I relished, but today, it was a necessity.

You seemed upset and agitated, throwing up your arms while you waited for your turn in line. Complaining loudly, you brushed my mother aside, "I'll pay for her," you barked. I looked at Mom, who made a slight, dismissive wave, as if accustomed to your outbursts, yet she maintained a serene smile.

"But you're not a hero," I whispered to her, my brow furrowed with concern.

I wasn't one to sugarcoat things, but even to me, it seemed harsh to label you so bluntly, especially in public. The crowd around us shifted, some casting curious glances, but mostly ignoring the unfolding scene as they were used to the eccentricities of city life.

"I'll just grab us some seats," Mom said, excusing herself, giving me a knowing look. As she moved away, she left me alone with you, standing ramrod straight and unyielding.

"No, I am a hero," you insisted, your voice raised a notch, drawing more attention. "I do things for others every day. Why can't she see that?"

I chewed on the inside of my cheek, feeling the weight of your words. Maybe there was some truth in them, but the way you put it—so loudly and in such a confrontational manner—it was all a little too flashy. My mind raced to find the words that might reach you, but before I could speak, a girl with a bright smile and kind eyes approached.

"Excuse me," she said gently, her gaze soft but firm, "but he is a hero. To me, he's a hero."

"We done here?" I asked exasperatedly.

The man in the lab coat looked up, a bit apologetically, "Just one more test for the day, please."

I rolled my eyes. "Okay, fine. Let's get this over with."

He led me to a large, metal chamber at the far end of the lab. "Now, remember, you only have a few attempts. When I give the signal, you’ll experience what we believe could be a temporary enhancement: the ability to double jump."

I eyed the chamber suspiciously. "Temporary? How temporary?"

"Hard to say," he admitted, adjusting his glasses. "Our theories suggest a few hours at the most."

"And how long have you been trying to figure this out?" I asked, curious.

"Years," he said with a smile that was half-excitement, half-frustration. "This could revolutionize not just athletics, but medicine and rehabilitation. The implications are enormous."

"Okay, let's do it," I decided, stepping into the chamber.

He closed the door behind me and began to explain the mechanics. "When I wave my hand, the floor beneath you will become active. Just focus, and on your command, you'll be able to jump higher than any human has ever jumped before."

I nodded, feeling a mix of nerves and thrill. "Ready when you are."

He waved his hand. "Now!"

Immediately, I felt a strange sensation beneath my feet. It was as if the very floor had become charged with electricity, yet it wasn't the typical tingle one associates with a shock; it was a warm, inviting energy.

On my command, I leaped into the air with a force I never knew I possessed.

I knew it. I fucking knew it. I knew it as soon as he put it in my hand. He forgot the fucking guacamole. Again. Jesus! No, wait, I think it was Juan today. Juan!

It was one of those lazy afternoons at Taco Joe's, where the air always seemed to buzz with the blend of fresh salsa and the laughter of contented customers. As a regular, I had developed an almost ritualistic routine: order, wait, devour, and then critique the various minor flaws with a love only a true aficionado could understand.

That day, my choice fell upon their legendary beast, the Diablo Burrito, stuffed with seasoned beef, rice, beans, cheese, and — oh, that crucial element — guacamole. But as I unwrapped the foil, the familiar rich green absence struck me. 

In a moment of rebellion, my hand took over before my brain could catch up. Instead of stuffing my mouth, I grabbed the nearest tool for unconventional investigation: a small plastic knife from the napkin dispenser. Before I could second-guess myself, I sliced open the burrito.
